answers.working:
RNA is made **complementary** and **antiparallel** to the template strand, and it carries U in place of T. So the RNA is the reverse complement of the template.

Read the template backwards (3' end first): C T C T T C G G A T C T G. Now pair each base (C with G, T with A, G with C, A with U): G A G A A G C C U A G A C. Written 5' to 3', the RNA is 5'-GAGAAGCCUAGAC-3'.

Option (B) simply copies the template with U for T, and option (D) is complementary but written in the wrong direction, so neither is the transcript. So the answer is option (A).

The trait appears in every generation, and every affected child has an affected parent, so it is **dominant**.

Now look at the affected fathers. The affected male in generation II had 1 daughter and 2 sons: the daughter is affected and both sons are normal. The affected male in generation III had 2 daughters and 2 sons: both daughters are affected and both sons are normal. So an affected father passes the trait to **all his daughters and none of his sons**. This is exactly what happens when the allele sits on the X chromosome: a father gives his X to every daughter and his Y to every son.

Affected mothers (generation I and the affected female in generation II) pass it to about half their sons and half their daughters, which also fits X-linked dominant inheritance. Autosomal dominant inheritance cannot be ruled out completely, but it would predict some affected sons from affected fathers, and none of the 4 such sons is affected. So the answer is option (A).

**Troponin** is a regulatory protein on the thin (actin) filament. When \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\) binds to troponin, it shifts tropomyosin and uncovers the myosin-binding sites on actin, so cross-bridges can form and the muscle contracts.

Insulin is a hormone that regulates blood glucose, myoglobin stores oxygen in muscle, and trypsin is a digestive enzyme. None of these acts directly in the contraction mechanism. So the answer is option (D).

The **epidermal tissue system** includes the epidermal cells, stomata with their guard cells and subsidiary cells, trichomes and root hairs. Bulliform cells of grass leaves are also modified epidermal cells.

The **Casparian strip** is a band of suberin in the walls of the **endodermis**, the innermost layer of the cortex of the root. It belongs to the ground tissue, not the epidermis. So the answer is option (B).

answers.value: The end products of meiosis II are haploid gametes.
answers.working:
In flowering plants, meiosis does **not** produce gametes directly. Meiosis in the anther gives haploid **microspores** (which develop into pollen grains), and meiosis in the ovule gives haploid **megaspores**. The gametes are formed later by mitosis inside the male and female gametophytes.

The other statements are true: crossing over and independent assortment make the four products genetically different; in most flowering plants only one of the four megaspores survives (monosporic development); and recombination happens in meiosis in both sexes. So the incorrect statement is option (C).

answers.value: Graph of Y against X: rising from the origin almost linearly, then levelling off into a flat plateau
answers.working:
At low light intensity, light is the **limiting factor**, so the rate of photosynthesis rises almost in proportion to light intensity. At higher intensity, other factors (such as \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) concentration or enzyme activity) become limiting, so the rate stops rising and levels off into a plateau.

A straight line forever (option C) ignores these other limiting factors, and the curve that falls back to zero (option A) is not the normal response over the usual range of light. So the answer is option (B).

**Pyruvate dehydrogenase** converts pyruvate to acetyl CoA in the **mitochondrial matrix**: Q - (iii).

**Lactate dehydrogenase** works in fermentation in the **cytoplasm**: R - (i).

**ATP synthase** is found in the inner mitochondrial membrane and in the **thylakoid membrane** of chloroplasts. Since (ii) is already used for P, the matching option uses the thylakoid membrane: S - (iv).

Plant P has \(n = 10\) and plant Q has \(n = 15\). The **embryo** is zygotic (one male + one female gamete), the **endosperm** is triploid (two polar nuclei from the female + one male gamete), and the **seed coat** comes from the integuments, so it has the mother's diploid number.

| Tissue | R (P female, Q male) | S (Q female, P male) |
|---|---|---|
| Embryo | \(10 + 15 = 25\) | \(15 + 10 = 25\) |
| Endosperm | \(2(10) + 15 = 35\) | \(2(15) + 10 = 40\) |
| Seed coat | 20 | 30 |

Only the embryo has the same number (25) in both crosses. So the answer is option (B).

ELISA and RT-PCR are used for other infections (ELISA for HIV, RT-PCR for RNA viruses), and gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments. So the answer is option (C).

answers.value: Circular plasmid vector with Ori and Amp\(^{R}\); EcoRI and BamHI sites both on the circle, away from Ori and Amp\(^{R}\)
answers.working:
When a plasmid is cut with **both** BamHI and EcoRI, the piece of plasmid between the two sites is removed and the gene is put in its place. The part that is kept must contain **both** the origin of replication (so the plasmid can copy itself) and the Amp\(^{R}\) gene (so transformed cells grow on ampicillin).

In option (A) and option (C), the two sites lie on opposite sides of the circle, so one piece holds Ori and the other holds Amp\(^{R}\): whichever piece is kept loses one of them. In option (B), the BamHI site lies inside Ori, so cutting there destroys the origin of replication.

In option (D), the two sites are close together on a stretch with neither Ori nor Amp\(^{R}\), so the large piece kept still has both. So the answer is option (D).

In PCR, the number of copies **doubles** in every cycle. Going back from the 30th cycle to the 20th cycle means undoing 10 doublings, that is, dividing by \(2^{10} = 1024\).

\(\dfrac{1\ \text{billion}}{1024} = \dfrac{10^{9}}{1024} \approx 9.8 \times 10^{5}\), which is about 1 million copies.

So the answer is option (C).

For **logistic growth**, the growth rate is

\(\dfrac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(\dfrac{K - N}{K}\right)\)

Substitute \(r = 0.01\), \(N = 400\) and \(K = 500\):

\(\dfrac{dN}{dt} = 0.01 \times 400 \times \dfrac{500 - 400}{500} = 4 \times \dfrac{100}{500} = 4 \times 0.2 = 0.8\)

So the population grows by 0.8 individuals per unit time, and the answer is option (B).

answers.value: Hemichordata is not considered as a chordate sub-phylum, and possesses a proto-notochord called stomochord.
answers.working:
Hemichordata was once treated as a sub-phylum of Chordata, but it is now placed as a **separate phylum** among the non-chordates. Hemichordates (such as *Balanoglossus*) have gill slits, but no true notochord: they have only a rudimentary structure in the proboscis called the **stomochord**, which looks like a notochord.

The water vascular system is a feature of echinoderms, not hemichordates, so option (A) is wrong, and options (B) and (C) are wrong because Hemichordata is no longer a chordate sub-phylum. So the answer is option (D).

answers.working:
Curve A lies to the **left** of B, so haemoglobin is more saturated at the same \(\mathrm{pO_2}\): oxygen binds more easily. A left shift happens with **low** \(\mathrm{[H^+]}\) (high pH), **low** \(\mathrm{pCO_2}\) and lower temperature, the conditions in the lungs.

Curve C lies to the **right**, meaning oxygen is released more easily. This happens at high \(\mathrm{[H^+]}\) (low pH) and high \(\mathrm{pCO_2}\), the conditions in the tissues. So option (B) wrongly links curve A to low pH, option (C) wrongly links curve C to low \(\mathrm{pCO_2}\), and option (D) is wrong because curve C shows weaker, not stronger, binding.

So the answer is option (A).
